vignette:
He is a 24-year-old Latin American man who comes to therapy after a man-made disaster changed the way he moves through the world. Before the event, he describes himself as steady and private, someone who preferred routines and long stretches of focused work. He lives alone, is single, and has built a life around structure: the same commute, the same coffee, the same quiet hours spent as a QA engineer, catching small errors before they become bigger problems. Friends have always known him as careful and observant, the kind of person who notices details others miss.

The disaster happens in a place he assumed was ordinary and safe. He is there when chaos erupts suddenly, with no time to make sense of it. He remembers the sound first, then the confusion, then the sharp awareness that people are panicking around him and that the normal rules of the day have disappeared. In the immediate aftermath, he moves on instinct. He helps where he can, follows instructions, and gets himself to safety, but later he cannot account for large pieces of what happened. In the days afterward, he keeps saying he feels "fine," but his body tells a different story. He jumps at loud noises, scans exits without thinking, and feels a wave of dread whenever he sees crowds gathering or hears sirens in the distance.

At work, he is still able to perform, but everything takes more effort. As a QA engineer, he spends his days looking for flaws, and that once felt like a natural extension of his mind. After the disaster, the same habit becomes less useful and more exhausting. He catches himself running worst-case scenarios on repeat, both in software and in life. If a system error appears, his stomach tightens as if another crisis is about to start. He rereads messages several times, not because he doubts his skills, but because his concentration breaks apart easily. He notices that he is slower to respond in meetings, not because he has nothing to say, but because he is busy checking the room, checking the door, checking his own body for signs of rising panic.

Sleep becomes one of the first things to unravel. He tries to go to bed at a reasonable hour, but when the lights are off and the apartment is quiet, the images come back with force. He lies awake replaying flashes of the event and imagining different endings, different choices, different ways he might have prevented more harm. Some nights he wakes with his heart pounding, convinced for a few seconds that he is back there. He keeps the television on low volume just to avoid the silence, though the noise sometimes makes things worse. In the mornings he feels depleted, like he has already worked a full day before he has even logged in.

He avoids reminders in ways that seem small at first and then shape his whole life. He changes routes so he will not pass by the site of the disaster. He stops watching the news after realizing a headline can unsettle him for hours. He turns down invitations to crowded places, telling friends he is busy or tired. He still wants connection, but he does not trust his own reactions in public. In conversation, he sometimes goes distant, as if part of him leaves the room when the topic shifts too close to the event. He notices that his patience is shorter now, and that he feels irritated by things that never used to bother him. Underneath that irritation is fear, though he rarely says so directly.

He also carries a painful sense of responsibility. Even when he knows, logically, that he did what he could, he keeps returning to the same questions: Why was he there? Why did he survive when others suffered more? What if he had acted faster? These thoughts come with a heavy guilt that he does not easily share. As a Latin American man, he has grown up with expectations to be composed, useful, and tough, and he has learned to handle distress alone. That habit now keeps him isolated. He tells himself he should be over it by now, should be stronger, should not be affected in such obvious ways.

Over time, he begins to recognize that he is not simply "stressed." He is living with his attention narrowed around danger, his sleep disrupted, his sense of safety damaged. Still, even in that state, he shows an earnest wish to keep going. He arrives to sessions on time, speaks carefully, and wants to understand why his mind keeps dragging him back to the disaster. He is not collapsed by what happened, but he is changed by it. The world that once felt orderly and predictable now feels fragile, and he moves through it with a vigilance that never fully turns off.
